source_read: PDF, American Journal of Epidemiology 157(3):273-278, all 6 pages read (pdftotext -layout); pp. 274-277 (methods, Figure 1, Tables 1-3, results on discordant deaths, multiple-cause codes) checked on renders at 150 dpi.

claims.overstatement: Mostly accurate. (1) '37 had been coded as natural deaths because poisoning was written only in Part II' turns the paper's 'typically' into 'all'; 'mostly because' would match. (2) That the 15 natural deaths were coded as non-dependent drug use 'because the certificate said use or abuse' is inferred from the coding rule in the Methods (code 305 when 'use' or 'abuse' is written); the paper does not report those certificates' words. (3) The 1,105 are all poisoning deaths, including alcohol, carbon monoxide and other non-drug agents, not drug deaths only; 7 of the 17 medical-investigator poisonings that vital statistics coded as other injuries were fire-related. (4) The medical investigator's remit excludes tribal and federal lands unless invited, a coverage limit the claim does not mention.
claims.note: Table 1 is internally consistent: 1,046 + 1,046 - 987 = 1,105; 1,046/1,105 = 94.7%; 987/1,105 = 89.3%; 59 discordant each way. The VS-only 59 break down as 24 + 13 + 15 + 2 + 3 + 2; the OMI-only 59 as 4 + 1 + 17 + 37. A fact the claim could use on how definitions change counts: including the multi-drug code E858.8 roughly doubles vital-statistics counts of unintentional illicit-drug overdose (339 to 609) and heroin overdose (273 to 537) deaths for 1995-1998. Neither source was treated as the reference standard; the authors recommend using both plus multiple-cause data.

anchors.extracted: New Mexico residents' poisoning deaths, 1995-1998: vital statistics 1,046, medical investigator (OMI) 1,046, both 987, either 1,105; each source alone held 94.7% of the union and both 89.3%. Only vital statistics captured residents who died out of state (24 over 4 years).

Of 59 vital-statistics poisoning deaths not classed as poisoning by the OMI: 24 occurred out of state; of the other 35, 13 (37.1%) were never reported to the OMI, 15 were natural deaths in OMI records (e.g., cirrhosis, sepsis, heart disease) coded as non-dependent drug abuse (ICD-9 305) in vital statistics, 2 were miscoded as non-poisoning by the OMI, 3 differed on undetermined manner and 2 were unspecified unintentional injuries in OMI records.

Of 59 OMI poisoning deaths not classed as poisoning in vital statistics: 4 (6.8%) were not found in vital statistics, 1 had a revised certificate never recoded, 17 (28.8%) were coded as other injuries (6 fire-related unintentional, 1 fire-related suicide), and 37 (62.7%) as natural deaths; these 37 typically named poisoning in Part II of the certificate but not in Part I; 16 of them were coded as other heart disease (ICD-9 420-429).

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods > Data sources > Medical examiner records; Definitions, 1st to 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: The OMI investigates sudden, unexplained, suspicious, violent or unattended deaths except on tribal and federal land (often invited there); every death suspected of being due to drugs, toxins or poisons gets a full autopsy and toxicology with confirmatory testing. Vital-statistics poisoning was underlying cause 305, E850-E869, E950-E952, E962 or E980-E982, coded by NCHS-trained nosologists: 'use' or 'abuse' gave 305; 'overdose', 'intoxication', 'toxicity' or 'poisoning' an E-code; a natural condition in Part I with a drug in Part II was coded as the natural condition unless it was a direct sequel of drug use.

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods, 1st paragraph (OMI codes); Surveillance data linkage
anchors.extracted: OMI deaths were retrieved by the OMI's own Manner of Death codes, assigned by investigators when entering pathologists' certificate information. Records were linked by hand on date of death, age, sex, race/ethnicity and name, allowing 1 day, 1 year and small spelling differences; unmatched deaths were then sought among non-poisoning deaths in the other file.

Including the multi-drug code E858.8 changed vital-statistics counts: unintentional illicit-drug overdose 609 with it against 339 without (OMI 526); unintentional heroin overdose 537 against 273 (OMI 360). Of vital-statistics E858.8 deaths, 72% matched an OMI death with a morphine, cocaine or methamphetamine code, and 55.6% an OMI illicit-overdose death with a morphine code.

claims.overstatement: Same two wording points as above. 'Coded as natural deaths because poisoning was written only in Part II' should keep the paper's 'typically'. 'Coded as drug use because of the certificate's words' is inferred from the stated coding rule, not reported for these 15 certificates. Both counts are of poisoning deaths of any agent, not of drug deaths only, and the medical investigator's classification is not validated as a reference.
claims.note: 37 and 15 confirmed on the rendered p. 276. In the same direction as the 37, vital statistics also coded 17 OMI poisonings as other injuries (some fire-related) and could not find 4.

anchors.extracted: Of 59 deaths the OMI classed as poisonings but vital statistics did not, 37 (62.7%) were coded as natural deaths, typically because poisoning appeared in Part II but not Part I of the certificate (16 as other heart disease); 17 (28.8%) as other injuries; 4 were not found and 1 had an unrecoded revised certificate.

Of 59 vital-statistics poisonings that the OMI did not class as poisoning, 15 (42.8% of the 35 in-state deaths) were natural deaths in OMI records (cirrhosis, sepsis, heart disease) coded as non-dependent drug abuse (ICD-9 305); 13 were never reported to the OMI; 24 occurred out of state.

anchors.locator: Materials and Methods > Definitions, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Coding rules behind both errors: code 305 (non-dependent drug abuse) when 'use' or 'abuse' is written on the certificate, which the poisoning definition counts; a natural condition in Part I with a drug only in Part II is coded as the natural condition unless it is a direct sequel of drug use.

anchors.locator: Results > Multiple-cause codes, 1st paragraph (starts p. 276); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (pp. 277-278) and 5th paragraph (limitations, p. 278)
anchors.extracted: E858.8 (unintentional poisoning by other drugs) names no single drug; with multiple-cause codes, 90% of New Mexico E858.8 deaths had an opiate, cocaine or amphetamine code and 85% an opiate code (US 88% and 83%), so 10-12% were not due to illicit drugs. These multiple-cause records were not linked to the OMI-vital statistics file.

key_findings.correction: Locator nuance only: the 72% sentence is printed on p. 276, but it closes the Results' 3rd paragraph, which starts on p. 275, so under the convention that paragraph counts on p. 275 (the 4th paragraph, with 55.6%, starts on p. 276). 270 fits both percentages (194/270 = 71.9%, 150/270 = 55.6%).

reporting_issues.note: Found independently: 72 + 118 - 56 = 134 and 109 + 173 - 72 = 210 against the printed 128 and 108; 339 + 526 - 277 = 588 against 480.
On the 150 dpi render of Figure 1 the 1994 heroin point (about 5.4) lies below the US point (about 6.6).

risk_of_bias.note: Moderate fits. The poisoning comparison that the claims use is the strongest part: manual linkage, discordant deaths reviewed both ways.

missed: 'Poisoning deaths' here are poisonings by any agent, not drug deaths only: the Introduction names carbon monoxide and alcohol (p. 274), and the definition spans E850-E869, which takes in non-drug substances and gases. So the 1,105 and the 59 discordant deaths each way are not all drug deaths, and claims should say 'poisoning deaths'. Of the 17 OMI poisonings coded as other injuries, 7 were fire-related (p. 276).

That the 15 OMI natural deaths were coded 305 'because of certificate wording' (card, interpretation_gap.results_show) is inferred from the coding rule on p. 274 ('use' or 'abuse' gives 305); the paper does not report those certificates' words. Likewise, the 37 deaths coded as natural 'typically', not always, had poisoning only in Part II.
